title: Vulkan 3D Rendering Engine
description:
Study of Vulkan's explicit, low-level rendering model, which trades the convenience of OpenGL's implicit state machine for direct control over — and direct responsibility for — nearly everything: GPU memory allocation, command buffer recording, and synchronization between the CPU and GPU and between GPU operations themselves, all things a driver handled invisibly under OpenGL.

The concepts worth studying in depth have no OpenGL equivalent: the swapchain (an explicit set of images the GPU renders into and the presentation engine displays, requiring manual management of which image is currently available versus being presented), pipeline state objects (nearly the entire GPU pipeline configuration baked into one immutable object up front instead of toggled per-draw-call, so the driver can precompile and optimize it once), and explicit synchronization primitives (fences for CPU-GPU sync, semaphores for GPU-GPU sync between queue operations).

The study focus is tracing one full frame's synchronization sequence in the reference implementation precisely — acquire swapchain image, wait on fence, record/submit command buffer with semaphore dependencies, present — since getting this sequence wrong is the single most common source of validation-layer errors and hard-to-debug rendering glitches when learning Vulkan.
architecture_overview: Instance/device setup (physical device selection, logical device + queues) → swapchain (presentable image set) → pipeline state objects (shaders, fixed-function state, baked immutable) → per-frame loop (acquire image [semaphore] → record command buffer → submit [wait/signal semaphores, fence] → present [wait semaphore]) → explicit GPU memory allocation for buffers/images throughout.

linked_node_explanations.Process Synchronization: Vulkan's fences (CPU–GPU) and semaphores (GPU–GPU) are explicit synchronization primitives with the same wait/signal semantics as classical OS synchronization, applied across the CPU/GPU boundary instead of threads.
linked_node_explanations.Memory Management and Virtual Memory: Vulkan requires manually allocating and sub-allocating GPU memory heaps for every buffer and image — a hands-on encounter with fragmentation, alignment, and allocation-strategy concerns usually only discussed for CPU virtual memory.
linked_node_explanations.ALU, Data-Path and Control Unit: Writing GLSL shaders that compile to SPIR-V and execute on the GPU's parallel compute units is a concrete look at a fundamentally different data-path/control-unit design (massively parallel, SIMT execution) than the single-instruction-stream model this topic usually assumes.

title: Zero-Trust Authentication Service Mesh
description:
Study of the zero-trust principle applied to service-to-service communication: instead of trusting traffic because it originates inside a perimeter, every request between services must independently authenticate and be authorized regardless of network location, meaning workload identity (proving which specific service is making a request, not just which IP) has to exist as a first-class concept.

SPIFFE/SPIRE's approach is worth studying precisely: every workload is issued a cryptographically verifiable identity document (an SVID, containing a SPIFFE ID) by a SPIRE agent, based on attestation — proving identity via something the platform can verify, like 'this process was started by Kubernetes with this specific service account,' not a static, stealable credential. These SVIDs then establish mutual TLS between services, where both sides present and verify each other's identity, not just the client verifying the server as in ordinary TLS.

The study focus is tracing how a service mesh like Istio automates mTLS enrollment and enforcement via sidecar proxies (Envoy) that transparently intercept and encrypt traffic without application code knowing mTLS is happening, and separately tracing SPIRE's attestation flow from workload startup to receiving a signed SVID, since this attestation step is what actually earns trust rather than assuming it.
architecture_overview: Workload startup → SPIRE agent attestation (verifies identity via platform-specific evidence) → SVID issuance (short-lived, cryptographically signed identity document) → mutual TLS handshake between services (both sides present + verify SVIDs) → authorization policy check → request proceeds or is denied, often enforced transparently by a sidecar proxy (Envoy) rather than application code.

linked_node_explanations.Application Layer Protocols (HTTP/HTTPS): Mutual TLS is ordinary TLS with an added client-certificate verification step, and tracing the extra handshake messages this requires is a direct, applied extension of standard HTTPS handshake knowledge.
linked_node_explanations.Process Synchronization: Short-lived SVIDs require automatic rotation before expiry without dropping in-flight connections, a real coordination problem between the identity-issuing agent and the workload's active TLS sessions.
linked_node_explanations.ISO/OSI and TCP/IP Protocol Stack: A sidecar proxy transparently intercepting and encrypting traffic between services is a concrete example of inserting a new function at a specific layer of the stack without changing the layers above it.
